title: All-photonic millimeter-wave and terahertz signal core at room and cryogenic temperatures
authors: Jiawen Liu, Chengli Wang, Aleksei Gaier, Tianyi Zhang, Gabriel Jülg, Yazan Lampert, André Garcia Primo, Alessandro Tomasino, Hua Li, Xin Ou, Ileana-Cristina Benea-Chelmus
abstract: Millimeter-wave and terahertz technologies offer new opportunities for high-capacity communications, sensing, and quantum systems, but electronic signal chains above 100 GHz are limited by weak sources, noisy receivers, and lossy interconnects. Photonic approaches mitigate these constraints by enabling chip-scale high-frequency components, yet existing implementations generally retain lossy off-chip electrical or free-space links, hindering dense and compact integration for cryogenic or space-constrained settings. Here, we show a monolithic lithium tantalate photonic chip, termed a signal core, which generates, modulates, routes, and detects continuous-wave signals at discrete frequencies between 100 GHz and 2.5 THz. The architecture integrates high-frequency functional modules on chip and uses exclusively fiber-based optical interfaces. Bidirectional coherent electro-optic conversion enables signal generation, detection, and nanosecond-scale amplitude and phase modulation, while micro-coplanar striplines interconnect the modules into an end-to-end signal chain on a single chip. Our modules achieve single-photon electro-optic coupling rates of g_0/2π=10 kHz and peak drive-power-normalized photon-flux conversion efficiencies of 1.0%/mW for generation and 0.5%/mW for detection. It also operates at 4 K in a dilution refrigerator through the same fiber-only optical links. Together, these capabilities establish an all-photonic platform for millimeter-wave-to-terahertz systems and offer a broadly applicable architecture for applications constrained by electrical-interconnect loss, heat load, and footprint.
summary: This paper presents an all-photonic signal core built on a monolithic lithium tantalate chip to address signal transmission limitations in the millimeter-wave and terahertz regimes. By integrating generation, modulation, and detection functions entirely on-chip using optical links, the system achieves high performance up to 2.5 THz, even when cooled to 4 K. This establishes a compact, low-loss platform for next-generation high-frequency quantum and classical applications.
main_problem: The primary challenge is overcoming the limitations of conventional electrical signal chains above 100 GHz for mmWave and THz applications due to inherent losses and noise.
main_result: The authors demonstrated an all-photonic signal core on a monolithic LiTaO3 chip capable of generating, modulating, routing, and detecting signals from 100 GHz to 2.5 THz using only fiber-based optical links.
method: The system utilizes bidirectional coherent electro-optic conversion within a chip architecture that integrates high-frequency functional modules using micro-coplanar striplines.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a monolithic lithium tantalate photonic chip acting as a signal core. It employs resonant enhancement via triply resonant converters to couple optical pumps to the microwave/THz signal, enabling end-to-end operation.
key_observables: Single-photon electro-optic coupling rates (e.g., 10 kHz), peak drive-power-normalized photon-flux conversion efficiencies (1.0%/mW for generation), and stable operation down to 4 K.
important_parameters: Operating frequency range (100 GHz to 2.5 THz), cryogenic temperature (4 K), and high field-enhancement factors (up to 121.8 for sidebands).
main_assumptions: The performance is governed by a trade-off between resonant coupling enhancement and signal loss, and the system relies on maintaining multiple spectral alignments (triply resonant condition).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison between electronic and photonic signal chains, the fabricated chip structure, and optical characterization showing loaded quality factors and spectral features.
paper_structure: The paper details the architecture, focusing on the resonant enhancement mechanism using DFG and electro-optic modulation. It presents measurements validating the performance at both room and cryogenic temperatures, analyzing power flow and coupling coefficients.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly integrated, chip-scale platform for high-frequency signal processing that bypasses electrical interconnect limitations, which is crucial for quantum sensing and quantum networking components operating at cryogenic temperatures.
